To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
'The new possibilities for women in export processing are that they can now earn wages, but the new problems are that they are paid low wages and are subject to a new form of exploitation.'
the growth of export manufacturing in Third World countries is not a sign of progress in the status of women.
the world market factories are not a solution to the problems of Third World women, but are rather a major cause of those problems.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the new export manufacturing industries on women workers in Third World countries.
the impact of the world market on the employment of women in Third World export manufacturing.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new possibilities for women workers in the export processing factories are limited to the extent that they are confined within the existing social relations of production.
the new export factories are not the panacea that some would have us believe, nor are they a disaster. They are a mixed bag. They do not necessarily offer a solution
the world market factories are not a solution to the problems of Third World women, but a new problem, a new form of subordination and exploitation of Third World women.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of export manufacturing in the Third World has been a process in which women are increasingly drawn into the labour market, but in such a way as to increase their subordination.
women are being integrated into the development process as a source of cheap labour power.
the world market factory, and the relations of production which characterize it, are part of a process which reproduces and deepens the subordination of women.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the new opportunities for women in export processing are not necessarily a progressive force in their lives, and that the problems of women workers in these factories are not simply the problems of workers in any other sector of the economy.

the subordination of women in Third World export manufacturing cannot be explained by the simple fact of their low wage levels, but by the fact that the work is organized in such a way as to be 'women's work'.

the subordination of women is not an inevitable consequence of their employment in export manufacturing. Rather, it has been actively created and maintained by the way in which women have been employed in these industries.
